newsitem.title: USA: Key Oklahoma bomb witness faces cross-examination.
newsitem.headline: Key Oklahoma bomb witness faces cross-examination.

text.p: A key prosecution witness in the Oklahoma City bombing trial faces a grueling cross-examination on Wednesday that will challenge her testimony that defendant Timothy McVeigh had told her he planned the attack.

Lori Fortier told a federal court in Denver on Tuesday how McVeigh had planned to bomb the Alfred P. Murrah federal building because he was angry about the assault on the Branch Davidian cult compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993.
Cult leader David Koresh and about 80 followers were killed in a fire at the compound after a botched FBI raid in 1993. McVeigh blamed the government for the deaths, Fortier told the court.

Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said it was "premature" to characterise Fortier's testimony as rehearsed. But when asked whether her remarks were damaging he said: "Wait until tomorrow and ask me then." He is expected to challenge her memory of the events going back to 1988 when she first met McVeigh.

In exchange for her testimony, the mother of two received immunity from prosecution at the trial of McVeigh, who is accused of planning and carrying out the April 19, 1995, bombing in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people.

Fortier's husband, Michael Fortier, is an old army buddy of McVeigh's and has entered into a plea agreement, admitting he knew McVeigh had planned the bombing but did nothing to stop it. McVeigh stayed with the Fortiers at their trailer home in Kingman, Arizona, during several visits, she testified.

Michael Fortier is in federal custody, facing up to 23 years in prison and is also expected to be a key witness for the prosecution. Defence attorneys have said they suspect the couple of collaborating on their testimony.

Lori Fortier told the court how she helped McVeigh forge a driver's license, that as soon as she heard about the bombing she "knew" it was McVeigh and how she now regrets taking no steps to try to prevent the tragedy.

The most riveting testimony came when she described how McVeigh put soup cans on the floor to show how he would build the bomb. "He placed the cans on the floor in the same arrangement he would place them in the truck," she said. "It would get the most impact that way," she said he told her.
In her testimony, Lori Fortier said she did not believe McVeigh would carry out his plan, partly because neither her husband nor co-defendant Terry Nichols wanted to help him.
"Tim was my friend and I thought he wasn't capable of this," she said.
But on the witness stand she said she now wished she would have done something to stop McVeigh.
Her comments brought little consolation to relatives of bombing victims.
"I'm angry with her because she could have saved them. She knows all it would have taken was one phone call," said Jannie Coverdale, who lost her two grandsons, Elijah and Aaron, in the bombing.
McVeigh stared at Lori Fortier throughout her testimony. He faces the death penalty if convicted. Nichols will be tried separately, at a later date.
Fortier also admitted to lying to Federal Bureau of Investigation agents soon after the bombing, despite her certainty that McVeigh was responsible.
"I didn't want to be linked to Tim in any way," she told the court.
